=== PROJECTS (11) ===
PROJECT: L.I.G.T.A.S. (Leakage Identification using Groundwater Testing and AI-based Sensing)
Page: /projects/ligtas
Tagline: A remote-controlled amphibious vehicle that checks floodwater for electrical leakage and sends alerts.
Status: Completed. Period: Aug 2025 – May 2026. Aldwin's role: Thesis Group Leader & Lead Hardware Developer.
Categories: Embedded Systems, Hardware, AI.
Stack: ESP32, C/C++, Python, Random Forest, LoRa, SIM800L GSM, React, Spring Boot, MySQL.
Summary: Floodwater can become energized when power lines fall into it, and flood monitors only track water level. L.I.G.T.A.S. is our thesis prototype: it drives into floodwater, measures voltage, classifies it as Safe or Danger with a Random Forest model (96.54% accuracy on the test set), and alerts responders by SMS and a live dashboard.
Overview: L.I.G.T.A.S. was our BSCpE thesis at PLM. Five of us built a small amphibious vehicle that can be driven into floodwater, read the voltage in the water, decide whether it is safe, and warn people before they wade in. I led the team and built the hardware and the microcontroller firmware.
Objective: Detect electrical hazards in floodwater and warn residents and responders in time, using parts a barangay could afford.
Problem: During floods in the Philippines, damaged power lines can energize the water, which adds an electrocution risk on top of drowning and property damage. Existing flood monitoring tracks water level and rainfall. It does not check for electrical leakage, and it is not mobile.
What Aldwin did:
- Led the five-member team through research, prototyping, testing and the thesis paper, and set the milestones.
- Designed and built the vehicle hardware: ESP32 boards, voltage and current sensing, GPS, IMU, a waterproof ultrasonic sensor, motor drivers, LoRa and GSM modules, and the power supply.
- Wrote the microcontroller firmware for sensing, motor control and communication on the vehicle and the handheld controller.
- Worked with the group on the other parts: the Random Forest model and the web dashboard were built by the team, and my hardware feeds both.
How it is built:
- Vehicle: Two ESP32 boards: one for sensing, motion and monitoring, one for communication. Sensors are a ZMPT101B voltage sensor, ACS712 current sensor, JSN-SR04T waterproof ultrasonic sensor, MPU9250 IMU and NEO-6M GPS. Two L298N drivers run the DC motors.
- Controller: A handheld unit with two ESP32 boards, a joystick, tactile switches, a real-time clock, an SD card for logging and a 3.5-inch LCD.
- Links: LoRa (SX1278) carries telemetry and drive commands. A SIM800L GSM module is the backup link and sends SMS alerts. A Wi-Fi camera streams video to a phone.
- Classifier: A Random Forest model using eight features per reading: voltage, voltage squared, a voltage zone, a danger score, a noise estimate, the change since the last reading, a five-reading average and the count of consecutive readings above 30 V.
Implementation notes:
- Voltage is sampled every 500 ms. A reading at or above 30 V counts as dangerous, and a three-reading debounce filter keeps a single spike from setting off a false alarm.
- The server also marks any reading above 30 V as DANGER before saving it, so a sensor or transmission fault cannot hide a hazard.
- The model was trained on 21,095 synthetic voltage samples (6,841 Safe and 14,254 Dangerous) with an 80/20 train and test split.
- SMS alerts go to contacts saved on the controller, and phone numbers are masked in the dashboard API.
Challenges and limits:
- The ZMPT101B reports an averaged (RMS) value, so a few short spikes were missed or misread in testing. The temporal features and the debounce filter reduce this, and the paper lists it as a known limit of the sensor approach.
- SMS was the weakest link, with 87.5% of alerts delivered. The paper recommends a backup alert channel.
- All testing was done in lab simulations and controlled trials, not in a real flood. The paper names real-flood testing as the next step.
Results:
- On 4,219 held-out samples the model reached 96.54% accuracy, 97.54% precision, 97.33% recall and a 97.44% F1-score.
- End-to-end classification time stayed under 100 ms.
- SMS alerts were classified correctly every time and took 5.32 seconds on average from reading to message.
- In a survey of 60 residents of flood-prone barangays in Manila, 96.7% found the system useful and 100% would recommend it for community use.
Awards:
- Top 2 Best Thesis
- Best Thesis Paper
- Best Booth
- Best Poster

PROJECT: KidVerse (KidVerse: A Magical World Edutainment for Growing Minds)
Page: /projects/kidverse
Tagline: A learning management system for nursery and kindergarten students, built for Wesleyan College of Manila.
Status: Completed. Period: August 2023 – May 2024. Aldwin's role: Full-Stack Developer.
Categories: Web Development, Software.
Stack: Node.js, MongoDB, REST API, JavaScript, HTML/CSS.
Summary: KidVerse is a web platform where children aged 5 to 7 take lessons and quizzes, teachers manage classes and grades, and parents help with enrollment. A five-person team built it for CPE Elective 1 at PLM, with Wesleyan College of Manila as the partner school.
Overview: KidVerse is an educational platform for children that blends learning with play, giving students and faculty dedicated portals for lessons, quizzes, grades and communication. It was built as a team project for CPE Elective at PLM, with Wesleyan College of Manila as the partner school.
Objective: Put lessons, quizzes and games on one platform that children can use, that teachers can manage without a developer, and that follows learning standards.
Problem: Young learners lose focus quickly and most online platforms are not designed for their age. Teachers have limited training with digital tools, and parents struggle to guide online classes while working. Many platforms also favor entertainment over actual learning content.
What Aldwin did:
- Full-stack developer in a five-member team. In the project plan I owned the faculty and student dashboards, the frontend and the backend.
- Built the Node.js REST API and the MongoDB data layer for accounts, courses, enrollment, grades, resources and chat.
- Built the student and faculty portals: enrollment with faculty approval, course and lesson pages, resource upload by link, a calendar for activities and deadlines, grade entry, and teacher-student chat.
- Worked with the team on UI design, testing and the research paper.
How it is built:
- Roles: Student (with parent access), Faculty and Admin, each with their own homepage.
- Student side: Enroll in nursery or kindergarten, open lessons and quizzes (Beginner and Advanced levels), play games, chat with teachers and edit a profile.
- Faculty side: Approve enrollment requests, manage subjects, add resources, set calendar activities, enter grades and chat with students.
- Process: Built with Feature-Driven Development, an Agile method, in short rounds: UI design, core features, then testing and bug fixing.
Implementation notes:
- Sign-up shows the privacy policy and terms of use before an account is created, since the users are children.
- Password recovery sends a one-time code to the user's email.
- The game page links out to ABCya, so the team did not build its own game engine.
Challenges and limits:
- Security was the main concern. The system stores children's data and the team had limited cybersecurity experience, which the paper lists as its first limitation.
- Keeping the platform an educational tool first. Too much entertainment weakens the lessons, so lessons and quizzes stayed the main path and games stayed secondary.
Results:
- Delivered working faculty, student and enrollment flows with chat, a calendar, grades, quizzes and games.
- The paper recommends next steps: a screen-time limit that notifies parents, a way for teachers to build their own games and quizzes, and stronger real-time chat.
Code: https://github.com/aldwinsamson/Kidverse

PROJECT: Fault-Tolerant AWS Web Architecture (Three-tier, multi-AZ web architecture on AWS)
Page: /projects/fault-tolerant-architecture
Tagline: A web architecture spread over availability zones, built with Terraform and CloudFormation.
Status: Completed. Period: Jun 2026 – Sep 2026. Aldwin's role: Cloud & DevOps Intern (solo, company task).
Categories: Cloud & DevOps.
Stack: AWS, Terraform, CloudFormation, VPC, ALB, NLB, RDS Multi-AZ, S3, KMS.
Summary: A three-tier AWS design built so that losing one availability zone does not take the application down. It has separate public, private and database subnets, load balancers for HTTP and TCP traffic, a multi-AZ database and hardened S3 storage. I built it as my final project at Stratpoint.
Overview: The goal was a design where each layer survives a failure in another zone, written as code so it can be rebuilt and reviewed.
Objective: Design, build and document a resilient web architecture on AWS that follows the Well-Architected Framework.
What Aldwin did:
- Designed the network: separate public, private and database subnets across availability zones, with internet gateways, NAT gateways and route tables.
- Set up Application Load Balancers for path-based HTTP and HTTPS routing and Network Load Balancers for TCP traffic to microservices.
- Provisioned a multi-AZ Amazon RDS database for the data tier.
- Hardened S3 buckets with lifecycle rules, encryption at rest with KMS and cross-region replication.
- Wrote the infrastructure as modular Terraform and CloudFormation templates and documented the design.
How it is built:
- Network: Public, private and database subnets in each availability zone. NAT gateways give private subnets outbound access.
- Traffic: ALB for path-based HTTP and HTTPS routing. NLB for high-throughput TCP services.
- Data: RDS in a multi-AZ setup, and S3 with lifecycle rules, KMS encryption and cross-region replication.
Results:
- The whole environment can be created from code, with the design and the steps written down for the next person.
Note: This is an internal company tool, so there is no public link or code.

PROJECT: 3-Tier App with GitOps Delivery (Task Manager: React, Node.js and PostgreSQL delivered by GitLab CI and Argo CD)
Page: /projects/3-tier-app
Tagline: A three-tier task manager that GitLab CI builds and Argo CD deploys to Kubernetes.
Status: Completed. Period: Jun 2026 – Sep 2026. Aldwin's role: Cloud & DevOps Intern (solo, company task).
Categories: Cloud & DevOps, Software.
Stack: React, Node.js, Express, PostgreSQL, Docker, GitLab CI, Helm, Argo CD, Kubernetes, Prometheus.
Summary: My capstone for the Stratpoint DevOps internship. A task manager in three tiers, packaged with Docker, built and published by a GitLab CI pipeline, and deployed to Kubernetes by Argo CD from a separate manifest repository. The backend exposes Prometheus metrics.
Overview: The app itself is simple on purpose. The work is in the delivery: a push to main produces versioned container images and an updated deployment config, and the cluster picks it up without anyone running kubectl or helm by hand.
Objective: Build a complete path from a code change to a running Kubernetes deployment, with every step automated and traceable.
Problem: Deploying by hand makes it hard to say what is running or which code produced it. I wanted every deployed image to point back to an exact commit, and I wanted the app repository to have no access to the cluster.
What Aldwin did:
- Wrote a Dockerfile for the frontend and the backend, plus a docker-compose file that runs the full stack locally with one command.
- Built the GitLab CI pipeline: two parallel jobs build and push the images, tagged with the commit SHA, then a second stage updates the image tags in the manifest repository.
- Kept the Helm chart and Kubernetes config in a separate manifest repository that Argo CD watches, so the app repository never touches the cluster.
- Added a /metrics endpoint to the Express backend with prom-client, for Prometheus.
- Stored the database password in a Kubernetes Secret, and kept the SSH key for the manifest push in a masked CI variable.
How it is built:
- Frontend: React task list UI, in its own container.
- Backend: Node.js and Express REST API with a Prometheus metrics endpoint.
- Database: PostgreSQL 17, with the schema and seed data in init.sql.
- Delivery: GitLab CI builds and pushes images to the GitLab Container Registry, then commits new tags to the manifest repo. Argo CD syncs the cluster to that repo.
Implementation notes:
- Images are tagged with the short commit SHA instead of latest, so any running image can be traced to the code that built it.
- The manifest update commit carries, so it does not start a second pipeline.
- The pipeline pushes to the manifest repo with an SSH key. A password in a CI script would end up in job logs, and a key can be revoked without changing the pipeline.
Challenges and limits:
- The first runner was a shell executor, and the build jobs failed with permission denied on the Docker socket. I switched to a Docker-executor runner and wrote that requirement into the README.
- The frontend container still runs the React development server. A production build would be the next improvement.
Results:
- Every push to main produces images tagged with the commit SHA and an updated manifest, and Argo CD deploys the change without manual kubectl or helm commands.
Note: This is an internal company tool, so there is no public link or code.

PROJECT: Portfolio Infrastructure on AWS (Terraform-built hosting and delivery for aldwinsamson.com)
Page: /projects/portfolio-aws-infrastructure
Tagline: Terraform-built S3 and CloudFront hosting with keyless deploys and monitoring. It ran this site and now stays in the repo as a switchable option.
Status: Completed. Period: Oct 2026 – Nov 2026. Aldwin's role: Cloud & DevOps Engineer (solo).
Categories: Cloud & DevOps.
Stack: AWS, Terraform, S3, CloudFront, ACM, Route 53, CloudWatch, GitHub Actions, Checkov, k3s, Argo CD, Prometheus, Grafana.
Summary: The hosting and delivery setup this portfolio ran on first, written as code. Terraform created a private S3 bucket served through CloudFront over HTTPS, GitHub Actions deployed it without stored AWS keys, security checks ran on every change, and a small k3s cluster ran Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana as a monitoring lab. The site now runs on Vercel's free plan, and the AWS setup stays in the repository so the domain can be pointed back at it.
Overview: I treated my own site as a production workload. Everything that ran it is in Terraform, the deploy pipeline had no long-lived AWS keys, and the repo has a runbook for deploys, rollbacks, costs and switching hosts.
Objective: Host a static site the way I would run a real one: repeatable, private by default, cheap and easy to roll back.
Problem: A static site does not need a server, but clicking it together in the AWS console would leave nothing repeatable and nothing to review. I wanted the setup to be code that someone else could read and rebuild.
What Aldwin did:
- Wrote the Terraform modules for storage, CDN with security headers, certificate and DNS, monitoring and the GitHub deploy roles, with one environment file holding the project name, domain, region and e-mail.
- Set up GitHub Actions to deploy through OIDC, so no AWS access keys are stored in GitHub. Infrastructure changes need my approval in a protected GitHub environment, and the site deploy role can only write one bucket and clear one CloudFront cache.
- Added checks to the pipeline: type check, tests, npm audit and Checkov scanning of the Terraform, with every skipped check explained in .checkov.yaml.
- Added production monitoring: a health check from six regions, CloudWatch alarms with e-mail alerts, and a monthly budget alert.
- Built a small k3s cluster with Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana to practice GitOps and monitoring.
- Wrote a runbook covering deploys, rollback, costs, troubleshooting and switching the domain between AWS and Vercel.
How it is built:
- Hosting: An S3 bucket with public access blocked, served only through CloudFront using origin access control. ACM and Route 53 provide HTTPS on the custom domain.
- Edge: A CloudFront Function maps clean URLs to index.html for the single-page app, and security headers are set at the edge. The Content Security Policy started in report-only mode and was enforced after I checked the browser console on every page.
- Deploy: GitHub Actions assumes an AWS role through OIDC. Assets upload first and index.html last, then the cache is invalidated and a smoke test runs.
- Lab: k3s on a small instance with Argo CD, Prometheus and Grafana, reachable only through AWS Systems Manager and kept separate from the production hosting.
Implementation notes:
- Rollback is a re-run of the deploy workflow with an older commit SHA.
- Controls I chose to skip, such as a web application firewall and bucket-level KMS, are written down in .checkov.yaml with the reason, instead of being ignored silently.
- I chose k3s over EKS because the EKS control plane alone lists at about $73 a month, which a static site cannot justify.
- One Terraform setting points the domain at AWS or at Vercel, so the AWS copy can stay deployed but idle.
Results:
- Ran the live site on this setup from launch until I moved it to Vercel's free plan to cut the monthly bill.
- The runbook estimated about $3 a month for production hosting, and about $18 to $20 with the lab running. These were estimates, not a bill.
- Moving to Vercel needed a vercel.json for the redirect rules and security headers, a small serverless function for the chatbot, and a DNS change. The site code itself has no AWS-specific parts.
- The modules are written so another environment, such as staging, needs a new environment folder and variables file but no module changes. I have not used that yet.
Code: https://github.com/aldwinsamson/Aldwin_Samson_Portfolio/tree/main/infra

PROJECT: Delay-Tolerant Role-Aware Messenger (DTRM: a LoRa field messenger that stores and forwards messages)
Page: /projects/delay-tolerant-messenger
Tagline: A battery-powered LoRa messenger that keeps messages until someone is in range.
Status: Completed. Period: October 2025. Aldwin's role: Hardware engineer & firmware developer (team of 8).
Categories: Embedded Systems, Hardware.
Stack: Arduino Uno R3, LoRa 433 MHz, SD card module, C/C++.
Summary: DTRM is a field messenger built on an Arduino Uno and a LoRa module. A user presses a button to send one of four preset messages. If a receiver is in range it shows right away, and if not, the message is saved and sent when another device or gateway appears. We built it for the Armed Forces of the Philippines as the intended user.
Overview: Field teams often work where there is no mobile signal or internet. DTRM is a small unit that sends short, predefined messages over LoRa and does not lose them when nobody is in range.
Objective: Keep vital messages moving in areas with limited or unstable connectivity, using affordable parts that are easy to buy locally.
Problem: Normal messaging fails without a stable network. In field and emergency work a message such as SAFE or SEND HELP still has to arrive, even if it arrives late.
What Aldwin did:
- Part of Group, a team of eight. I handled the hardware engineering and the microcontroller firmware.
- Assembled the hardware: an Arduino Uno R3, a LoRa module with a 433 MHz antenna, tactile buttons, an SD card module and a battery, in a clear case.
- Wrote the firmware that encodes a button press, sends it over LoRa, and keeps the message in storage when no receiver answers.
How it is built:
- Messages: Four preset messages: SAFE, SEND HELP, ENEMY SPOTTED and AFFIRMATIVE.
- Modes: Real-time delivery when a receiver is in range, and delay-tolerant store-and-forward when it is not.
- Priority: Messages are prioritized by the sender's role.
- Hardware: Arduino Uno R3, LoRa module, 433 MHz antenna and cable, tactile buttons, SD card module, battery and case.
Implementation notes:
- A message that cannot be delivered is stored. When another device or a gateway is detected, it is forwarded automatically.
- No internet or mobile network is needed. LoRa handles the radio link between nearby units.
Results:
- Delivered a working prototype that combines real-time and delay-tolerant messaging in one low-cost unit.

PROJECT: SumoBot (Bluetooth-controlled sumo robot)
Page: /projects/sumobot
Tagline: A phone-controlled sumo robot that took 2nd place in a school competition.
Status: Completed. Period: September 2025. Aldwin's role: Hardware engineer & firmware developer (team).
Categories: Embedded Systems, Hardware.
Stack: ESP32, L298 motor driver, DC motors, Bluetooth, C/C++.
Summary: A sumo-fighting robot our team built and drove in our school's competition. An ESP32 runs two DC motors through an L298 motor driver and takes commands from a phone app over Bluetooth. It won 2nd place.
Overview: A small robot built to push another robot out of a ring. A person drives it from a phone, so the work was in the hardware, the motor control and a reliable Bluetooth link.
What Aldwin did:
- Part of a team. I handled the hardware engineering and the microcontroller firmware.
- Wired the ESP32, the L298 driver and two DC motors, and wrote the code that turns phone commands into motor movement.
- Set up the mobile app connection to the robot over Bluetooth.
How it is built:
- Controller: ESP32 microcontroller.
- Drive: L298 motor driver and two DC motors.
- Control: A mobile app connected to the robot over Bluetooth.
Results:
- Won 2nd place in our school's sumo robot competition.
Awards:
- 2nd place, school sumo robot competition
